newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak C.bank governor says will keep crown stable.
newsitem.headline: Slovak C.bank governor says will keep crown stable.

text.p: National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) Governor Vladimir Masar on Thursday reaffirmed the central bank's commitment to maintaining a stable economy and currency.

In an interview with the official TASR news agency, Masar said a gradual decline in inflation and maintenance of the crown's exchange rate stability "within the set fluctuation band" remained the two key monetary goals of the NBS.

"The NBS's independence guarantees that monetary policy will take a direction which will not lead to risking the currency's destabilisation. This aim will also be a signal to foreign investors that Slovakia's currency and economy is worthy of their confidence," he said.

Slovakia's economy has proved resilient despite a turbulent political scene, with gross domestic product (GDP) growing 7.0 percent, year-on-year, for the first three quarters, and annual inflation at just 5.4 percent in November.

But analysts have warned that the government's 1997 budget, with a deficit planned to increase to at least 36.9 billion crowns ($1.35 billion) from the planned 27 billion crown deficit in 1996, could endanger the stability of the crown.

Masar tried to allay any fears of currency destabilisation because of the deficit, saying: "According to law, the NBS should support the government's economic policy in a way which would not endanger the currency's stability."

On January 1, the NBS widened the crown's fluctuation band against its mark/dollar basket midpoint to plus/minus seven percent from five percent in an attempt to introduce more currency risk to the crown and deter the inflow of "hot money".
The NBS has long been battling a burgeoning money supply and the inflationary pressures it brings, which have been fuelled in part by speculative funds flowing into the country.
Announcing the bands, Masar said the NBS was prepared to use their full extent to keep the money supply in check.

The NBS's key M2 money supply had grown by 19.0 percent in September, down from 22.1 percent in the same month of the previous year. The NBS originally forecast M2 expansion of 11.6 percent, year-on-year, for 1996, but recently admitted it was more likely to be 16-18 percent.
